reasoning: Quote is verbatim (TL;DR, line 919), and the same compression appears in the shipped prose ('SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line across anxiety disorders, OCD, and PTSD', line 975), exactly as the finding states. Read as the free-standing card it is rendered as, it licenses an SNRI as first-line OCD pharmacotherapy, which is off-guideline: APA (2007, reaffirmed) and NICE treat SSRIs (often at higher-than-depression doses) as first-line for OCD with clomipramine next, and SNRI evidence in OCD is limited. The page contradicts its own overlay three times — key points ('OCD: exposure and response prevention plus a higher-dose SSRI'), the embedded quiz (keyed 'Higher-dose SSRI + ERP'), and the exam anchors ('OCD is treated first-line with ERP and an SSRI... clomipramine or antipsychotic augmentation... refractory') — so a learner acting on the TL;DR could pick venlafaxine for OCD and be wrong by the page's own standard. The replacement is accurate and appropriately scoped: SNRIs as alternatives for anxiety disorders and PTSD (consistent with the page's own listing of venlafaxine among PTSD options and VA/DoD practice) but not OCD, at the right level for both audiences.

Quote is verbatim (overlay key point, line 29). The internal contradiction is exact: the shipped prose (line 90) states stopping maintenance medication 'nearly triples postpartum relapse (pooled ~35% overall; ~66% off medication vs ~23% on prophylaxis),' and the page's listed evidence source is wesseloo-2016-postpartum-relapse. Those figures match Wesseloo et al., Am J Psychiatry 2016 (postpartum relapse 66%, 95% CI 57-75, after discontinuation vs 23%, 95% CI 14-37, on prophylaxis) — a ~2.9x difference, i.e., a near-tripling. The card's 'roughly doubles' halves the strongest effect size on the page and is the version a learner quotes on rounds; the same card ships to residents. The replacement restates the card with the correct multiplier and the two anchoring percentages, matching both the page prose and the cited paper, and stays level-appropriate. Judged from knowledge; the figures are settled and independently corroborated by the page's own prose, so no PubMed lookup was needed.

Quote is verbatim (line 315). The problem is real and internally demonstrable: the same page's Management paragraph (line 319) teaches means restriction — 'remove or secure firearms' — as the most evidence-based single intervention, the student tasks and pearls repeat it ('means restriction — firearms and lethal medication above all — is the highest-yield single intervention'), yet the risk-stratification paragraph files firearm access under static factors that 'cannot be changed' and omits it from the dynamic/modifiable list. Under VA/DoD CPG (2024) and standard risk-formulation teaching, lethal-means access is precisely the modifiable factor lethal-means safety targets; a learner following the quoted sentence would present firearm access on rounds as unmodifiable baseline rather than the highest-yield intervention target. The replacement is correct and well-crafted: it preserves the true static factors, keeps the point that firearm access raises baseline risk, and makes the modifiability the explicit bridge to means restriction — appropriate for MS3s and residents.

Quote is verbatim (line 448). The construct error is real: threat/control-override as defined by Link & Stueve (1994) and operationalized by Swanson et al. (1996) is the combination of threat delusions (others intend harm) with control-override symptoms (outside forces overriding one's internal self-control — thought insertion, mind control); command hallucinations are a separate risk marker, not part of TCO. The page's parenthetical equates the named construct with 'persecutory delusions paired with command hallucinations,' teaching a wrong definition; notably the library's own violence.html tool string lists 'persecutory delusions, command hallucinations, threat/control-override' as three distinct items, consistent with the correction. The finding is also right to note (in basis, not as a required text change) that the MacArthur follow-up (Appelbaum et al. 2000) found TCO delusions did not predict violence in discharged patients, so the construct should not anchor the definitional high-risk claim. The replacement is well-judged: it retains the defensible bedside heuristic (command hallucinations the patient feels compelled to obey are a genuine concern, and the page's pearls repeat it without the TCO label) while demoting TCO to a related-but-distinct construct with its correct definition — accurate and level-appropriate for both audiences. Judged from knowledge; the definitions are settled.
